title_guess: UPSC Prelims 2025 economy questions solved by looking up the matching course lectures
running_examples: Q4 figures: revenue expenditure ₹80,000, revenue receipts ₹60,000, borrowings ₹10,000, interest ₹6,000 -> revenue deficit 20,000, fiscal deficit 10,000, primary deficit 4,000
Q5 figures: fiscal deficit ₹50,000, interest ₹1,500 -> gross primary deficit ₹48,500 (₹10,000 non-debt receipts are a distractor)

20th livestock census counts shown with up/down arrows per animal

best_moments.why: deficit as a gap: a red expenditure bar runs past a shorter green receipt bar, the missing piece becomes a 'gap' block named fiscal deficit, which then splits into four ways to fill it
elimination made visible: once statement II is crossed, every answer option that contains II is crossed too, leaving one option ticked
devolution criteria fan into one stacked bar whose coloured slices are sized by weight, so 'tax effort is a small slice' is seen, not read
progress circles 1-6 in the side panel turn green as each question is finished: a simple per-question tracker
a loan arrow from lender to government gets a red 'liability' ring and a return arrow (principal + interest): why borrowings are capital receipts

weak_moments.why: Q5 is a numeric question but no working is drawn; the page sits still for about 30 s before the answer is ticked
live footage of a hand scrolling app menus on a tablet: promotional, small text, little teaching
mission purpose shown as paragraph text on a small tablet screen inside the frame
intro is a promotional count of how many paper questions the channel's courses covered

segments.teaches: Q1 (government receipts): statement I, capital receipts create a liability or reduce assets, is true, checked against the lecture's receipts tree

segments.teaches: Q1 statement II: borrowings (and disinvestment) are capital receipts; a loan creates a liability repaid with principal and interest

elements.what: tablet lecture: capital-receipt list with borrowings highlighted
lender box (within India / foreign) -> loan arrow -> government emblem
red 'liability' ring on the loan arrow; return arrow labelled principal + interest
green highlighter and tick on statement II

segments.notes: the lecture explains 'liability' with a two-way money picture (loan in, repayment out)
segments.idea: borrowed money must be paid back with interest, so it is a liability and a capital receipt
segments.shown_as: on the tablet a lender box (inside India / foreign) sends a loan arrow to the government emblem; a red ring on the arrow says liability and a return arrow says repay principal plus interest; cut back and statement II gets the green stripe and tick

segments.teaches: Q1 statement III is false: interest the government receives on loans it gave is a non-tax revenue receipt, not a liability; answer (a) I and II only

elements.what: tablet lecture: revenue receipts split into tax and non-tax; non-tax bullets incl. PSU dividends and interest received on loans
red cross on statement III; green tick on option (a)

segments.idea: interest coming in to the government is income (revenue), not a debt
segments.shown_as: the tablet lecture opens the revenue-receipt branch (tax and non-tax), and under non-tax a bullet for interest received on loans the government gave; cut back: statement III gets a red cross, option (a) a green tick, and circle 1 in the side panel turns green

segments.teaches: Q2 (IBRD): statement III, set up to help rebuild Europe after World War II, is true, shown by the lecture's war-destruction timeline

segments.teaches: Q2: later the IBRD's scope widened to long-term, low-interest loans to (mainly middle-income) countries for human and infrastructure development, so statement I is true; statement II (works single-handedly against poverty) is false

segments.shown_as: the lecture shows a bank building with a money bag sending a long arrow to a stacked bar of country income groups under a globe, the big middle-income block receiving it; two lists hang below (human development, infrastructure); cut back: statement I gets a green tick and statement II a red cross

segments.teaches: Q2 answer (c) I and III only; a side note from the lecture shows lending to private companies is the IFC's job

segments.shown_as: a short tablet cut shows another bank building passing a money bag to a cluster of private-sector buildings in a developing country; cut back: option (c) is ticked and circle 2 turns green

segments.teaches: Q4 (deficit numbers): fiscal deficit equals what the government must borrow, so 'fiscal deficit = ₹10,000' (the borrowings) is true

elements.what: Q4 page with four rupee figures and three statements
hand opens the public-finance chapter, deficit lecture
budget briefcase with a red total-expenditure bar and a shorter green total-receipt bar
'gap' block at the end of the green bar named fiscal deficit
deficit financing splits into external aid, external borrowing, internal borrowing, printing money
debt-financing list numbered 1-4; a stack of notes flows to the government emblem as external aid
green tick on statement II

segments.notes: strongest picture in the video: deficit = missing length of a bar, then the ways to fill it
segments.idea: the fiscal deficit is the gap between spending and income, and it is filled by borrowing
segments.shown_as: Q4 lays out four rupee figures; on the tablet a budget briefcase sends out a long red bar (total expenditure) over a shorter green bar (total receipt); the missing piece at the end of the green bar becomes a 'gap' block named fiscal deficit, which drops an arrow into deficit financing and splits into four ways to fill it; a stack of notes then flows to the government emblem as external aid; cut back: statement II ticked
segments.example: revenue expenditure ₹80,000; revenue receipts ₹60,000; borrowings ₹10,000; interest ₹6,000

segments.teaches: Q4 statement I: revenue deficit = revenue expenditure - revenue receipts = 80,000 - 60,000 = 20,000, true

elements.what: hand opens the budget lecture
receipt notes -> government emblem -> expenditure notes
both split into a revenue budget box and a capital budget box
side line: actual data, provisional estimates, budget estimates by year
revenue receipt - revenue expenditure -> '-ive' arrow -> revenue deficit
green tick on statement I

segments.notes: no arithmetic is drawn; the lecture gives the rule and the narrator applies it
segments.idea: revenue deficit is the shortfall inside the revenue box only
segments.shown_as: on the tablet, receipts flow into the government emblem and expenditure flows out; both split into a revenue box and a capital box; inside the revenue box, receipts minus expenditure gives a minus arrow that drops to 'revenue deficit' (a side timeline marks actual, provisional and budget-estimate years); cut back: statement I ticked

segments.teaches: Q4 statement III: primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments = 10,000 - 6,000 = 4,000, true; answer (d) all three

elements.what: tablet lecture: total receipt vs total expenditure, '+ive' surplus budget and '-ive' deficit budget
fiscal deficit = total expenditure - total receipt (excluding borrowing); primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest on past borrowing
green tick on statement III and on option (d)
progress circle 4 turns green

segments.notes: rule shown as text formulas next to a stamped budget icon
segments.idea: remove the interest on old debt from the fiscal deficit and you get the primary deficit
segments.shown_as: the tablet lecture puts total receipt and total expenditure side by side: plus means surplus budget, minus means deficit budget; a stamped budget icon then shows two formulas (fiscal deficit = spending - receipts; primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest on past borrowing); cut back: statement III ticked, option (d) ticked, circle 4 green

segments.teaches: Q5: gross primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest = 50,000 - 1,500 = 48,500; non-debt capital receipts are a distractor; answer (a)

elements.what: Q5 page: one numeric question with four rupee options
green tick on option (a)
progress circle 5 turns green

segments.notes: no lecture cut-away and no working on screen; reuses the primary-deficit rule from Q4 (an exam_link chain between questions)
segments.idea: the same primary-deficit rule solves a numeric question; ignore figures the rule does not use
segments.shown_as: Q5 stays on screen for about half a minute with no picture or working drawn; then option (a) is ticked and circle 5 turns green
segments.example: fiscal deficit ₹50,000 - interest ₹1,500 = ₹48,500; ₹10,000 non-debt receipts not used

segments.teaches: Q6 (15th Finance Commission): vertical devolution is 41% of the divisible tax pool, so statement II (45%) is false; options containing II are eliminated, leaving (c)

segments.idea: states get 41% of the central tax pool, so a 45% claim is wrong, and that alone removes three options
